title: Other common and important disorders
content:
Other common and important disorders

Figure 3.6.1. Melasma
Bilateral brown pigmented patches on the face, especially on the cheeks, nose bridge
and forehead
Seen more in women than in men
Sun exposure, pregnancy, oral contraceptive pills and other risk factors trigger onset and
progression
Figure 3.6.2. Vitiligo
Loss of pigment-producing cells or melanocytes from the skin that determines the
different tones of skin and hair colour
Affects skin anywhere in the body
Occurs at any age, progressive
Affects 0.5%–2% of the population
Figure 3.6.3. Basal cell carcinoma
A common type of skin cancer originating from keratinocytes (skin cells)
Typically appears as a slowly growing plaque or nodule
May gradually enlarge to form a mass that bleeds easily
Usually localized and rarely spreads (non-invasive)
Commonly occurs on sun-exposed areas of the body
If suspected, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation and management
Figure 3.6.4. (left) and 3.6.5. (right) Squamous cell carcinoma
A common type of skin cancer originating from squamous cells (skin cells)
Typically presents as a slowly growing plaque or nodule
May enlarge to form a mass that bleeds or ulcerates easily
Unlike basal cell carcinoma, it can be invasive and may spread to other parts of the body
(metastasize)
Risk factors include chronic ulcers (from injury, burns, or disease), sun exposure,
smoking, and aging
If suspected, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation and management
Figure 3.6.6. Melanoma
Most serious type of skin cancer
Skin cancer of pigment-producing cells
Affects skin anywhere in the body
Warning signs: asymmetric, uneven border, various shades of black, changes in
size/shape/colour/appearance
If suspected, refer immediately to a specialist
Figure 3.6.7. (left) and 3.6.8. (right) Severe drug eruption (Stevens–Johnson
syndrome/Toxic epidermal necrolysis)
Serious reaction caused by medication
Usually develops during the first 1–2 weeks after starting the causative medication
Often begins with a painful rash
Blistering and peeling of the skin and mucous membranes (mouth, nose, eyes, genitals)
as it progresses
Flu-like symptoms (fever, sore mouth/throat, etc.) may appear before skin/mucous
membrane involvement
If suspected, refer immediately to a specialist
Stopping the causative medication is the most important
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Use of medicated creams and ointments
content:
Use of medicated creams and ointments

Topical medications are effective in treating many of the skin diseases. It is important to remind
patients to wash their hands before and after applying the creams. Typically, it is recommended
that a thin layer of the ointment be applied and the cream massaged to the affected areas.
Regarding the amount of medication to use, one can opt for the "fingertip unit", which is the
amount of ointment or cream needed to reach from the fingertip to the first crease of the finger.
This is approximately equal to 0.5 grams. Thus, you can use the image below to estimate how
many "fingertip units" are recommended for each body part.
Figure 3.7.1. Steps for applying topical treatment
Wash hands: Start by washing your hands thoroughly with soap and water to ensure
they're clean before touching the affected area.
Apply treatment: Apply a thin layer of the treatment to the affected area. Avoid using
too much cream, as a thin layer is usually sufficient. The amount to be applied can be
estimated using the 'finger-tip-unit'.
Massage gently: Gently massage the treatment into the skin using circular motions.
Wash hands: After applying the treatment, wash your hands again to remove any
residue and prevent accidental transfer to other areas.
Fingertip unit guide:
Fingertip unit: 1
Per arm: 3
Front: 7
Back and buttocks: 7
Per hand: 1
Per leg: 6
Per foot: 2
Remember that different medicated creams may have unique application
instructions, so always read and follow the guidance provided on the product
packaging and any advice given by your healthcare professional.
For scabies treatment, do not wash the hands after applying the ointment or
cream, as the hands are one of the most commonly affected areas and need
adequate exposure to the medication.
It is important to note that each medication may have different instructions for use. Therefore,
reading the medication's specific guidance prior to use is recommended.
Caution should also be exercised regarding the overuse of certain medications, especially
topical corticosteroids. Topical steroids are typically used for eczema, psoriasis, and other
inflammatory skin diseases. Self-administration of topical steroids can be dangerous and should
not be used without medical advice. While steroids can be helpful in reducing itchiness and
inflammation, long-term use has various side-effects, including delayed wound healing, thin skin
that bruises easily and infections.
Side-effects of topical steroids Prolonged or inappropriate use of topical steroids may cause
the following side effects:
Skin-related effects: thinning of the skin, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or
hyperpigmentation, stretch marks (especially in armpits or groin), easy bruising or
tearing of the skin, increased hair growth or thickness, redness
Hormonal effects: round face ("moon face") as seen in Cushing syndrome
Other effects: worsening of skin infections, risk of bone weakening and fractures
In children: slow growth with long-term use
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: When making a referral
content:
When making a referral

If you are unsure of the diagnosis, consider referring the patient. When immediate referral is not
possible, take clear photos of the skin lesion(s) for later review. Photos are valuable tools that
support accurate diagnosis of skin conditions. Referral should also be considered when you
suspect a serious disease or when further examination is necessary to confirm the diagnosis.
To ensure an effective referral, especially when done remotely (e.g. via telemedicine), it is
important to provide more than just a photo. Use the same approach described in this booklet
for describing skin lesions. Whenever possible, include the following information in your referral
notes:
Onset: When did the symptoms start? Was the onset sudden (acute), gradual
(subacute), or prolonged (chronic)?
Skin lesions: What types of lesions are present (e.g. papules, ulcers, patches)? Are
multiple types present?
Texture: Is the lesion soft, firm, scaly, crusted, dry, or moist?
Distribution: Where are the lesions located? Are they on one or both sides? Localized
or widespread? Symmetrical or asymmetrical?
Sensation: Is the lesion itchy, painful, or numb? Is there any loss of sensation?
You may also include additional observations such as warmth, discharge, or smell, as well as
symptoms beyond the skin, such as fever, joint pain, or swelling, that may help guide diagnosis
and treatment.
Wounds are common, especially in remote communities. They may result from a variety of
causes, such as injury, burns, infections, or underlying medical conditions, but regardless of the
cause, the basic principles of wound care remain the same. Proper wound care is essential to
prevent infection, support healing, and reduce the risk of long-term complications such as
scarring or disability.
This chapter begins with the fundamentals of wound care, followed by guidance on assessing
the cause of wounds and additional tips to promote healing. Wound care techniques can be
taught to patients and their families, so that care can continue where they live.
You can also refer to ANNEXURE 5 where it provides a flow chart to help guide wound care.
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Basics of wound care
content:
Basics of wound care

There are five main principles to support and accelerate the wound healing process.
1.​ Wash the wound
2.​ Keep the wound moist
3.​ Timely dressing change
4.​ Remove dead skin, tissues and any foreign objects
5.​ Diagnose and treat infection early
1. Wash the wound
Keep the wound and surrounding skin clean by washing with clean water or a saline solution.
Wash gently. This is to wash away any bacteria or debris from the surface of the wound. Avoid
using hydrogen peroxide, alcohol or iodine products. These products may damage the newly
growing cells to heal the wound. It is also important to wear gloves, but if they are not available,
wash your hands very well with soap and water before and after touching the wound.
If you are worried that the water may not be clean, boil the water. Cool it down before using it on
the wound. Clean water means that it should be fit for drinking.
2. Keep the wound moist
The wound should not be too dry or too moist. As it is also composed of living cells such as
those in any other parts of our body, it needs some moisture for the new skin tissue to grow and
close the wound. A moist wound environment is not only good for wound healing, but it also
helps in relieving pain.
If the wound surface is dry, an ointment can be applied. Petroleum jelly is one of the best and
inexpensive ointments to apply on a wound. However, it may not always be available. Other
products or natural sources (honey, turmeric, aloe vera, etc.) can be used in community settings
as alternatives. If you are unsure about what you have is appropriate for application on a
wound, consult a specialist.
3. Timely dressing change
Wound dressings help maintain a moist environment at the wound surface, which supports
healing. Use clean gauze or cloth to cover the wound. The frequency of dressing changes
depends on the wound condition and the type of dressing used. In general, dressings should be
changed once a day or whenever they become wet or dirty.
If the wound produces excessive exudate – moisture that leaks onto the surrounding skin and
causes maceration – the dressing should be changed more frequently. For clean wounds that
are healing well, less frequent dressing changes (such as a few times per week) may be
sufficient.
Maceration
For effective wound healing, the skin around the wound (called the periwound area)
must remain healthy. Excessive exudate (fluid) from the wound can damage this
surrounding skin. Maceration happens when too much exudate makes the nearby
skin look whitish, soft, or soggy. This is a sign that the dressing may need to be
changed more often to protect the skin and support proper healing.
4. Remove dead skin and tissues and any foreign objects
Dead skin and tissues must be removed to support healing – this process is called
"debridement". Debridement can be done surgically in a sterile way with sterile sharp
instruments or, if available, chemically with ointments which help dissolve dead tissues. If bone
is exposed or can be felt, this is a strong indication of possible osteomyelitis (bone infection)
and the patient should be referred to a specialist for further evaluation and possible removal.
Any foreign objects, such as nails, small stones, or wood splinters, can also interfere with
wound healing and must be removed. People affected by leprosy or diabetes, who often have
reduced sensation, may not feel pain and therefore may not notice these objects.
Do not debride dry and intact black eschars with no evidence of infection.
5. Diagnose and treat infection early
Infection can delay wound healing. Not only it may make wound healing stagnant, it may even
worsen the wound, leading to a longer time to heal. It is therefore important to diagnose and
treat infection as early as possible.
A wound may be infected if:
it becomes red, swollen, hot, and painful;
it has pus; or
it starts to smell bad.
The infection may be spreading to other parts of the body if:
the patient has a fever;
there is lymphangitis (inflammation of the lymphatic channels); or
lymph nodes (felt as lumps in the neck, armpits, or groin) become swollen and tender.
In such cases, treat the patient with systemic antibiotics. Wash the wound thoroughly with clean
water and increase the frequency of dressing changes.
When a patient is experiencing fever and chills, suspect sepsis, which is a serious condition
that the body is over reacting and causing extreme response to the infection. The patient may
also present with altered mental status or low blood pressure (hypotension). Refer the patient
immediately to a doctor.
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Assess and correct cause(s) of wound
content:
Assess and correct cause(s) of wound

Assessing and treating the underlying disease or condition are crucial for providing patients
with the right care. Wounds can occur due to various causes, ranging from trauma and burns
(external causes) to infectious to non-infectious ones (internal causes).
If it is an internal cause, treatment and management of the cause are as important as wound
care to achieve complete healing. If these causes are not managed well, it can lead to delayed
wound healing. For example, if you do not manage the blood sugar level in a patient with
diabetic foot ulcer, the wound will likely lead to a long healing course. If you see a patient with a
wound from skin tuberculosis, you need to treat for tuberculosis, only then the wound will heal.
Certain external factors can delay wound healing. For example, pressure ulcers require relief of
pressure at the wound site through frequent position changes. This is especially important for
people with diabetes or leprosy, who often have reduced sensation in their limbs.
Without normal sensation, pressure may be unevenly distributed, particularly on the soles of the
feet, resulting in wounds. In such cases, off-loading devices such as specially designed shoes
or supports are needed to reduce pressure on specific areas and allow the wound to heal.
Additionally, underlying systemic illnesses, such as anaemia, diabetes, peripheral arterial
disease (PAD), hypothyroidism (a type of autoimmune disease) and HIV/AIDS, as well as some
therapies, such as use of corticosteroids, can lead to wound healing delay. A range of daily
activities, from smoking to eating habits, can also cause wound healing delay. Understanding
the presence of these underlying conditions and correcting them are also important.
If you suspect any underlying condition from internal causes or are unsure about the cause of
the wound, refer the patient to a specialist.
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Additional tips to help wound healing
content:
Additional tips to help wound healing

Manage swelling... Swelling (oedema) can slow down wound healing. For wounds on the lower
limbs, encourage patients to elevate the affected limb to reduce swelling. Compression
bandaging and gentle massage may also support the reduction of oedema and promote faster
healing.
Prevent or treat physical sequelae/disability... Wound care should aim not only for wound
closure, but also for the preservation of physical function. Patients should not be discouraged
from moving the body part affected by a wound. Instead, encourage early and safe movement
from the beginning of treatment. Prolonged immobility can lead to muscle wasting and loss of
strength, making it harder for patients to regain movement even after the wound has healed.
Advise and provide appropriate mobility aids such as crutches, walkers, or adaptive equipment,
and teach both patients and caregivers how to use them safely. Tailor these strategies to the
available resources and cultural context of the community.
Incorporating these approaches during wound care is vital to preventing physical disabilities and
helping patients maintain independence and quality of life.
Eating healthy... Good nutrition is essential for wound healing. Ensure the patient is eating a
balanced diet with adequate protein, fruits, and vegetables to support tissue repair and recovery.
Continue care after wound closure... Even after the wound has healed, care must continue. A
scarred area remains vulnerable to breakdown or recurrence of a wound. To keep the skin
healthy, apply petroleum jelly or moisturizing cream regularly to keep the skin soft and hydrated.
Also avoid putting pressure on the scar area whenever possible.
When to consider referral... If the size of a wound does not show improvement within 4–6
weeks, this indicates that additional care may be needed, and referral to a specialized facility is
recommended. Always refer the patient if the wound worsens at any point. To make informed
decisions, it is important to monitor the wound's progress by regularly taking photographs or
measuring its size and depth.
In conclusion, effective wound care requires a holistic approach. Healing depends not only on
direct wound management but also on the patient's overall health, daily practices, and living
conditions. Engaging the patient and their family in the care process is essential to ensure
adherence to treatment and to improve long-term outcomes.
Healthy skin is everyone's right – free from diseased skin. While some skin conditions, such
as atopic dermatitis, are unavoidable due to genetic predisposition, others, like injuries or
infections, may result from environmental factors such as climate, overcrowding, or poor living
conditions. These challenges are often difficult to overcome quickly.
However, many skin diseases can be prevented or better controlled through community-level
actions. Education and awareness play a crucial role. Because skin diseases are often visible,
people affected may face stigma and discrimination, which can harm both their physical and
mental health. With the right knowledge and support, communities can challenge
misconceptions and promote inclusion.
This chapter offers practical approaches for educating patients, families, and communities to
improve skin health and to support the elimination of skin-related neglected tropical diseases
(skin NTDs).
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Skin care: Key habits for healthy skin
content:
Skin care: Key habits for healthy skin

This section outlines simple, everyday practices that help maintain healthy skin and prevent
common skin conditions and infections. These key messages can be easily shared with
patients, families, and communities.
1. Daily self-care practices
These are the most important day-to-day actions that everyone can take:
Wash hands regularly – especially before eating and after using the toilet.
Bathe daily with soap.
Moisturize after bathing to prevent dry skin.
Trim fingernails regularly.
Why it matters: Clean and well-cared-for skin is essential to prevent infections, not
only of the skin, but also of the gut, eyes, lungs, and other parts of the body.
2. Keeping clothes, bedding, and surroundings clean
Regular washing of personal items and bedding is important for skin health and
infection/infestation prevention:
Clothing: Wash any soiled clothing prior to wearing. Avoid strong soaps and detergents
that may irritate the skin.
Bedding: Wash sheets and blankets at least once every week, or every two weeks. If
available, use a vacuum cleaner to remove dirt from your bedding. Hang or spread
sheets and blankets under direct sun regularly. Sunlight is a natural disinfectant and
helps kill germs.
General hygiene: Keep sleeping and living areas clean and well-ventilated. Remove
accumulated dust, sweat, and body fluids that can promote bacterial or fungal growth.
Why it matters: Clean clothes, bedding, and surroundings reduce the risk of skin
infections, infestations such as scabies, and allergic reactions caused by dust and
irritants.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Protection from the sun
content:
Protection from the sun

The sun's ultraviolet (UV) rays can damage the skin over time, leading to sunburn, premature
aging, and an increased risk of skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
and basal cell carcinoma. Protecting the skin from the sun is therefore an important part of
maintaining long-term skin health.
Simple steps to protect the skin from sun damage:
Apply sunscreen before going outdoors, especially exposed areas like the face, arms,
and legs.
Wear sun-protective clothing, such as hats or long-sleeved shirts.
Limit time in direct sunlight by avoiding outdoor activities during peak sunlight hours (10
a.m. to 4 p.m.), and seek shade whenever possible.
It is very important to share these tips with anyone who spends a significant amount of time in
the sun, including agricultural workers and fishermen.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Protection from insect bites
content:
Protection from insect bites

Preventing insect bites is an important prevention method not only for avoiding discomfort, but
also for protecting oneself from getting infected with diseases spread by insects or for reducing
the risk of allergic reactions.
Simple steps to be protected from insect bites:
Wear protective clothing: Use long-sleeved clothing and pants, especially in areas with
high mosquito activity or in regions where insect-borne diseases are prevalent.
Use insect repellents: Apply insect repellents containing DEET, picaridin or other
recommended ingredients to exposed skin. Reapply as needed, especially during the
evening when mosquitoes are most active.
Avoid attractants: Avoid using heavily scented products and brightly coloured clothing
that may attract insects.
Use bednets and screens: In areas or housings where insects are a concern, use
bednets and screens to create a protective barrier.
Exercise caution in specific environments: Keep your surroundings clean to minimize
or eliminate breeding sites of vectors, such as stagnant water, tall grass and dense
vegetation as well as domestic water containers in your house.
Seek medical attention: In cases of severe reactions to insect bites or suspected
exposure to disease-carrying insects, seek immediate medical attention.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Seeking care at an early stage
content:
Seeking care at an early stage

Encouraging patients to check their skin
"Look, ask and feel" is not only a helpful tool for a provider when assessing skin lesions, but it is
also something that patients can adopt for protecting themselves. Encourage patients to look at
their skin often for any new or rapidly changing lesions. Further, if there are any lesions or areas
that are hard to be looked at by the patients themselves (such as their back), have them ask a
trusted family member or a friend to take a closer look. Finally, encourage them to feel the lesion
for an irregular or raised texture. If it does feel irregular or raised, the patients should seek
medical care.
Keeping first-aid supplies at home
Keep first-aid supplies, such as plasters and dressings, readily available at home. This can
prevent exposing the wound to dirt and germs at the earliest to stall secondary infections.
More awareness and seeking care at an early stage
Skin lesions are so common in the community that many people neglect the conditions. They
may think these are "a part of their lives"; they do not think that this is something for which they
should seek care or which can be treated. This can lead to delays in treatment and serious
complications. There needs to be a higher level of awareness about skin infections so that
people will seek earlier care. Similarly, there is lack of awareness about the fact that many of
these conditions can be prevented by maintaining good skin hygiene and taking care of any
known wounds. Assess your community's awareness of skin hygiene and educate.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Approaches to reducing stigma and discrimination
content:
Approaches to reducing stigma and discrimination

Many skin diseases, particularly when they affect visible parts of the body, can lead to stigma
and discrimination. This is especially true for skin NTDs, such as leprosy, which have been
among the most stigmatized conditions. However, many other skin diseases face similar
challenges.
Stigma and discrimination, often rooted within the community, are driven by misconceptions,
fear of contagion and social prejudices. In some cases, stigma may lead to isolation, affecting
not only patients but also their families. Self-stigma, wherein an individual internalizes the
negative attitudes of others, can be especially harmful, as it impacts the patient's mental
well-being and reduces his/her willingness to seek care.
You play a pivotal role in combating stigma as a health-care provider. It is important that you
treat patients with skin NTDs and other skin conditions with dignity and respect, ensuring that
your own attitudes do not contribute to the stigma. By demonstrating empathy and
professionalism, you can set an example for others in the community.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Empowering patients to take action
content:
Empowering patients to take action

As providers, it is essential to encourage patients to take action and care for themselves, as
self-care is a big part of good skin health.
Share these five key goals with your patients and answer any questions that they may have with
regard to achieving these goals:
1.​ Prove to others that you are able to take care of your skin: Ensure that patients have
a solid understanding of good skin hygiene.
2.​ Prove to others that you are able to prevent disability: It is important that patients
know and use preventive techniques (such as wearing protective shoes, applying
sunscreen and performing wound care), and prioritize including these steps in their daily
lives to maintain good skin health.
3.​ Prove that you can make your life a good example for others to follow: By adopting
these practices, patients can become a steward and encourage others to also follow
these steps.
4.​ Find ways to help other people: Completing skin checks, encouraging good skin
hygiene practices and helping others to treat their wounds can be some of the ways in
which patients can help their community members. With this united effort, patients can
support one another and the efforts of promoting skin health grow stronger. Additionally,
patients can also become community advocates for promoting policy changes and
expansion of public health efforts.
5.​ At all times, remember that you are special: Living with a skin disease can take a
great mental toll, especially for diseases that carry stigma in the community.
Encouraging love for self is fundamental to the success of skin disease treatment.
Conclusion
This booklet adopts a skin sign and symptom-based approach to skin NTDs and other skin
diseases, moving beyond the traditional disease-specific focus, often found in previous training
materials. By emphasizing the recognition of the syndromes and patterns instead of just
individual diseases, this approach is designed to better align with your day-to-day clinical
practice, helping you to identify and manage a broad range of skin conditions.
For any disease control efforts to be successful, community engagement is vital. Because most
skin diseases do not cause immediate death, they are often overlooked by communities.
Sensitization to improving the skin health of the community is crucial. As a front-line health-care
worker, you are at the forefront of this effort to bring about a positive change. Your role goes
beyond diagnosing and treating patients with skin diseases – you have a unique opportunity
to motivate, educate and engage your community in preventing skin diseases and
promoting early access to care.
If the health-seeking behaviour is such that an individual accesses health-care facilities when
he/she first notices his/her abnormal skin condition, there will be fewer delays in diagnosis and
treatment of skin NTDs and other debilitating skin diseases. The skin, too frequently
overlooked, is an important indicator of overall health and maintaining healthy skin
contributes to the well-being of the entire community.
As you continue your essential work, this booklet is intended to be a practical resource to
support you in improving skin health in your communities. We hope it equips you with the
knowledge and confidence needed to manage skin NTDs and other skin diseases effectively,
thereby helping reduce the burden of skin diseases in the regions where you serve.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: ALGINA (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
ALGINA
Manufacturer: Genuone Sciences/Westmont [UNILAB, Inc] — Non-Rx
Composition: Per 10 mL Na alginate 500 mg (as dry 425 mg), Na bicarbonate 213 mg, Ca carbonate 325 mg
Indications: Symptomatic treatment of gastroesophageal reflux eg, acid regurgitation, heartburn & indigestion due to reflux of stomach contents.
Dosage: Adult & childn ≥12 yr 10-20 mL up to qid. Childn 6-11 yr 5-10 mL.
Administration: Take after meals & before bedtime.
Special Precautions: Hypersensitivity. Low Na diet; CHF, edema, or cirrhosis; hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis. Discontinue if symptoms worsen or do not improve after 7 days. Renal failure. Childn <6 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Na alginate: Anaphylactic reaction/shock; bronchospasm; bloating, flatulence; urticaria. Na bicarbonate: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis; arrhythmia; apnea; bloating, flatulence; tiredness. Ca carbonate: Alkalosis, decreased appetite, hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, milk-alkali syndrome; dizziness, headache; burping, constipation, flatulence, nausea, rebound hyperacidity, vomiting; weakness.
Interactions: May decrease absorption of other minerals eg, Ca, Zn, Mn, chromium & Mg. May interfere w/ absorption of other medicines. Decreased absorption of tetracyclines; digoxin, indomethacin; Fe salts; antifungals (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole); azithromycin, nitrofurantoin, rifampicin, phenytoin, chloroquine, phenothiazine antipsychotics (eg, chlorpromazine) & bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate, etidronate, risedronate). May decrease excretion of weakly basic drugs (eg, quinidine, chlorpromazine, propranolol, diazepam) & increase excretion of acidic drugs (eg, phenytoin, pentobarb, warfarin). Changes in urine pH, increased urinary excretion & decreased of blood conc of salicylates eg, aspirin. Formation of insoluble metal ion chelates w/ fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin & ofloxacin) & penicillamine (for RA). Na alginate: May decrease absorption of Ca, Zn, Mn, chromium, & Mg if used concomitantly. Na bicarbonate: Increased rate of naproxen absorption.
Presentation & Packing: Oral susp (sachet) 10 mL x 100's.

title: ANERDIC (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
ANERDIC
Manufacturer: PT Dexa Medica [Glorious Dexa Mandaya] — Non-Rx
Composition: DLBS2411 Cinnamomum burmannii (Nees & T. Nees) Blume (Indonesian cinnamon bark)
Indications: Symptomatic relief of gastritis, heartburn & gastric hyperacidity.
Dosage: 1-2 tab daily.
Presentation & Packing: Tab 250 mg x 30's (P1,620/box).

title: FULZIMED (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
FULZIMED
Manufacturer: Medhaus — Non-Rx
Composition: Ca carbonate 800 mg, Mg hydroxide 165 mg, famotidine 10 mg
Indications: Short-term symptomatic relief of heartburn or non-ulcer dyspepsia. Relief of hyperacidity & as a daily source of extra Ca.
Dosage: 1 tab daily.
Administration: Take 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals. Chew tab completely before swallowing.
Special Precautions: Flatulence & alkalosis may occur. Concomitant use w/ ketoconazole & itraconazole.
Adverse Reactions: Hypercalcemia. Mg hydroxide: Diarrhea, hypermagnesemia. Ca carbonate: Constipation.
Interactions: Administer antacid 2-3 hr apart. CYP450 inhibitors. May reduce absorption of ketoconazole & itraconazole.
Presentation & Packing: Chewable tab 32's (P320).

title: GAVISCON (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
GAVISCON
Manufacturer: Reckitt Benckiser — Non-Rx
Composition: Per tab Na alginate 250 mg, Na bicarbonate 133.5 mg, Ca carbonate 80 mg. Per 10 mL oral susp Na alginate 500 mg, Na bicarbonate 267 mg, Ca carbonate 160 mg
Indications: Symptoms of GERD eg, acid regurgitation, heartburn due to reflux of stomach content.
Dosage: Tab Adult & childn >12 yr 2-4 tabs. Susp Adult & childn >12 yr 10-20 mL.
Administration: Take after meals & at bedtime. Chew tab thoroughly before swallowing.
Presentation & Packing: Chewable tab 8's (P16.50/tab). Oral susp (bottle) 150 mL (P285/bottle), (sachet) 10 mL (P28.50/sachet).

title: GAVISCON DOUBLE ACTION (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
GAVISCON DOUBLE ACTION
Manufacturer: Reckitt Benckiser — Non-Rx
Composition: Per tab Na alginate 250 mg, Na bicarbonate 106.5 mg, Ca carbonate 187.5 mg. Per 10 mL oral susp Na alginate 500 mg, Na bicarbonate 213 mg, Ca carbonate 325 mg
Indications: Symptoms of GERD eg, acid regurgitation, heartburn & indigestion eg, following meals or during pregnancy & for symptoms of excess stomach acid (hyperacidity).
Dosage: Tab Adult & childn ≥12 yr 2-4 tab up to qid. Susp Adult & childn ≥12 yr 10-20 mL up to qid. Childn <12 yr Should be given only on medical advice.
Administration: Take after meals & at bedtime. Chew tab thoroughly before swallowing.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Moderate or severe renal insufficiency.
Special Precautions: Patients on highly restricted salt diet eg, CHF & renal impairment; w/ hypercalcaemia, nephrocalcinosis & recurrent Ca-containing renal calculi; phenylketonurics. May mask symptoms of other serious, underlying medical conditions. Oral susp: May cause allergic reactions due to methyl parahydroxybenzoate & propyl para hydroxybenzoate.
Adverse Reactions: Anaphylactic & anaphylactoid reaction. Hypersensitivity reactions eg, urticaria; resp effects eg, bronchospasm.
Presentation & Packing: Chewable tab 8's (P18.50/tab). Oral susp (sachet) 10 mL (P31/sachet).

title: GELTAZINE (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
GELTAZINE

title: KREMIL-S COOL RELIEF (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
KREMIL-S COOL RELIEF
Manufacturer: UNILAB, Inc — Non-Rx
Composition: Na alginate 500 mg (as dry 425 mg), Na bicarbonate 213 mg, Ca carbonate 325 mg
Indications: Gastroesophageal reflux eg, acid regurgitation, heartburn, & indigestion due to reflux of stomach contents.
Dosage: Adults & childn ≥12 yr 10-20 mL up to qid. Childn 6-11 yr 5-10 mL.
Administration: Taken after meals & before bedtime.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Low Na diet; CHF, renal failure, edema, or cirrhosis.
Special Precautions: Hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis. Discontinue if symptoms worsen or do not improve after 7 days. Renal failure. Not recommended in childn <6 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Na alginate: Anaphylactic reaction/shock; bronchospasm; flatulence; urticaria. Na bicarbonate: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis; arrhythmia; apnea; bloating; flatulence; tiredness. Ca carbonate: Alkalosis, decreased appetite, hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, milk- alkali syndrome; dizziness, headache; burping, constipation, flatulence, nausea, rebound hyperacidity, vomiting; weakness.
Interactions: May decrease absorption of other minerals eg, Ca, Zn, Mn, chromium & Mg. May interfere w/ absorption of other medicines. Decreased absorption of tetracyclines; digoxin, indomethacin, Fe salts; antifungals (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole); azithromycin, nitrofurantoin, rifampicin, phenytoin, chloroquine, phenothiazine antipsychotics (eg, chlorpromazine) & bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate, etidronate, risedronate). May decrease excretion of weakly basic drugs (eg, quinidine, chlorpromazine, propranolol, diazepam) & increase excretion of acidic drugs (eg, phenytoin, pentobarbital, warfarin). Changes in urine pH.

title: KREMIL-S (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
KREMIL-S
Manufacturer: UNILAB, Inc — Non-Rx
Composition: Al hydroxide 178 mg, Mg hydroxide 233 mg, simeticone 30 mg
Indications: Symptomatic relief of hyperacidity associated w/ peptic ulcer, gastritis, esophagitis & dyspepsia. Antiflatulent to alleviate the symptoms of gassiness including post-op gas pain associated w/ hyperacidity. Adjunct to H2-blockers or proton pump inhibitors for rapid relief of ulcer symptoms.
Dosage: Adult 1-2 tab.
Administration: Take 1 hr after each meal & at bedtime. Swallow whole w/ water. May be chewed then swallow w/o water.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Kidney disease, intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, fecal impaction, gastric outlet obstruction, constipation, phosphate depletion & low serum phosphate, osteomalacia.
Special Precautions: Risk of Al & Mg accumulation & toxicity w/ advanced kidney disease. Phenylketonurics. Concomitant use w/ other medicines. Consult if to use for >14 days. Pregnancy & lactation.
Adverse Reactions: Diarrhea or constipation.
Interactions: May decrease absorption of tetracycline & Fe; take tetracycline 1 hr before or 2 hr after antacids & 2 hr before or 3 hr after Fe- containing prep. May decrease absorption of oral digoxin or indomethacin, INH, quinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin), ketoconazole. May increase urinary excretion due to changes in urine pH & decrease blood conc of salicylates eg, aspirin. Increase in basic drugs may decrease excretion of weakly propranolol, diazepam, chlorpromazine, quinidine of weakly acidic drugs (eg, phenytoin, pentobarbital, warfarin). May increase absorption of dicumarol, diazepam & pseudoephedrine. May decrease the rate of chlordiazepoxide absorption. May reduce the bioavailability of biphosphonates (eg, alendronate, etidronate, risedronate).
Presentation & Packing: Chewable tab 1's (P9.25/tab), 100's (P925/pack), 4's (P37/pack), 500's (P4,625/pack).

title: KREMIL-S ADVANCE (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
KREMIL-S ADVANCE
Manufacturer: UNILAB, Inc — Non-Rx
Composition: Famotidine 10 mg, Ca carbonate 800 mg, Mg hydroxide 165 mg
Indications: Relief of heartburn associated w/ acid indigestion & hyperacidity.
Dosage: Adult & childn ≥12 yr 1 tab daily as needed. Max: 2 tab/day.
Administration: Take 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals. Chew tab completely before swallowing.
Special Precautions: Hypersensitivity. Trouble or pain swallowing food, vomiting w/ blood or bloody black stools. Patients using other acid reducers; heartburn for >3 mth. Frequent chest or shoulder pain w/ shortness of breath, lightheadedness, sweating, or dizziness may occur. Stomach pain, nausea & vomiting & unexplained wt loss. Moderate (CrCl <50 mL/min) to severe (CrCl <10 mL/min) kidney disease.
Adverse Reactions: Famotidine: constipation, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal & gas-related discomfort, decreased appetite, dry mouth, heartburn & loss of taste; skin reactions; headache, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, muscle weakness, seizures, insomnia, drowsiness, depression, confusion, disorientation, anxiety, decreased sexual desire, & hallucinations; kidney problems (eg, increased serum creatinine conc & abnormal amounts of protein in the urine) & liver disease (jaundice). Fever, HTN, flushing, muscle cramps, pain in the joints, tinnitus & community-acquired pneumonia. Antacids: Flatulence; Ca carbonate; high Ca & Mg levels in the blood in patients w/ kidney impairment; alkalosis.
Interactions: May cause formation of complexes that are not absorbed w/ propranolol, INH, prednisolone, diflunisal & naproxen. Decreases absorption of tetracycline & Fe.
Presentation & Packing: Chewable tab 1's (P22.50/tab), 100's (P2,250/pack).

title: MAALOX PLUS (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
MAALOX PLUS
Manufacturer: Opella Healthcare — Non-Rx
Composition: Per chewable tab Al hydroxide 200 mg, Mg hydroxide 200 mg, simethicone 25 mg. Per 5 mL susp Al hydroxide 225 mg, Mg hydroxide 200 mg, simethicone 25 mg
Indications: Symptomatic relief of hyperacidity & as an antiflatulent to alleviate the symptoms of gas, including post-op gas pain.
Dosage: Chewable tab Chew or suck 2-4 tab qid. Susp 10-20 mL qid.
Administration: Take 20 min-1 hr after meals & at bedtime. Tab: Chew well.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. State of cachexia (general wasting away of the body), porphyria, severe forms of kidney failure. Childn.
Special Precautions: Accelerated intestinal transit may occur; do not use as long-term treatment. May cause constipation; intestinal blockage at high doses. Patients on low-P diet. Contains methylparaben & propylparaben which may cause allergic reactions. Avoid use w/ tetracycline. Diabetic patients on a reduced-calorie diet. Avoid prolonged use in patients w/ severe forms of kidney failure. Pregnancy & lactation. Oral susp: Do not take >80 mL in a 24-hr period or max dose for >2 wk.
Adverse Reactions: Occasionally, diarrhea or constipation.
Interactions: Reduced GI absorption of tetracyclines. Increased blood quinidine levels. Al hydroxide: May reduce absorption of H2 antagonists, atenolol, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, chloroquine, diflunisal, digoxin, bisphosphonates, ethambutol, fluoroquinolones, Na fluoride, glucocorticoids, indomethacin, INH, kayexalate, ketoconazole, lincosamides, metoprolol, phenothiazine neuroleptics, penicillamine, propranolol, Fe salts. Increased Al levels w/ citrates particularly in patients w/ kidney failure.

title: MONNAX/MONNAX PLUS (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:

Indications: Monnax Symptomatic relief of hyperacidity. Monnax Plus Chewable tab: Reduction of gastric hyperacidity. Relief of bloating commonly associated w/ hyperacidity & other conditions. Antiflatulent to alleviate the symptoms of gassiness including post-op gas pain associated w/ hyperacidity. Adjunct to H2-blockers or PPIs for rapid relief of ulcer symptoms.
Dosage: Chewable tab Adult 1-2 tab. Oral susp 10-20 mL qid.
Administration: Chewable tab: May be chewed then swallowed w/o water or swallowed whole w/ water. Take 1 hr after each meal & at bedtime. Oral susp: Take 20 min-1 hr after meals & at bedtime.
Contraindications: Patients suffering from kidney failure. Chewable tab: Hypersensitivity. Patient w/ kidney disease; intestinal obstruction; appendicitis; fecal impaction; gastric outlet obstruction; phosphate depletion & low serum phosphate; osteomalacia. Not to be used during pregnancy unless considered essential.
Special Precautions: Not to be used during pregnancy unless considered essential. Chewable tab: Patients on low Mg diet. Avoid taking any other medicines w/in 2 hr before or 2 hr after administration. Do not take at max doses for >2 wk in a row. Breastfeeding. Do not give to childn <12 yr. May cause central nervous depression in presence of renal insufficiency & should be used w/ caution in patients w/ advanced renal disease. Long-term exposure to high doses may lead to encephalopathy or worsen dialysis osteomalacia in patients w/ renal impairment. Avoid prolonged use in patients w/ renal failure.

May decrease absorption of orally administered digoxin or indomethacin, INH, quinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin), ketoconazole. Antacid-induced changes in urine pH increase urinary excretion & decrease blood conc of salicylates eg, aspirin. Antacid-induced increases in urine pH may decrease excretion of weakly basic drugs (eg, quinidine, chlorpromazine, propranolol, diazepam) & increase excretion of weakly basic drugs (eg, phenytoin, pentobarbital, warfarin). Increased absorption of dicumarol, diazepam & pseudoephedrine. May decrease the rate of chlordiazepoxide absorption. Reduced bioavailability of bisphosphonates (eg, alendronate, etidronate, risedronate). Oral susp: May increase serum levels of quinidine. Al(OH)3: May form complexes resulting in decreased absorption w/ tetracyclines, digoxin & vit. May prevent proper absorption of H2-antagonists, atenolol, chloroquine, cyclines, diflunisal, digoxin, diphosphonates, ethambutol, fluoroquinolones, Na fluorine, glucocorticoids, indomethacin, INH, kayexalate, ketoconazole, lincosamides, metoprolol, neuroleptics, phenothiazines, penicillamine, propranolol, Fe salts.

title: BUSCOPAN PLUS (Antacids, Antireflux Agents & Antiulcerants)
content:
BUSCOPAN PLUS
Manufacturer: Opella Healthcare — Non-Rx
Composition: Hyoscine-N-butylbromide 10 mg, paracetamol 500 mg
Indications: Relief from pain of stronger abdominal cramps including menstrual cramps & urinary tract spasm.
Dosage: Adult 1-2 tab tid. Max: 6 tab daily.
Administration: Swallow whole w/ sufficient amount of water, do not chew.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Myasthenia gravis, mechanical stenosis in the GIT, paralytical or obstructive ileus, megacolon, severe hepatocellular insufficiency (Child-Pugh C); rare hereditary conditions.
Special Precautions: Seek medical advice in case of persisting severe, unexplained abdominal pain w/ symptoms eg, fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movement, abdominal tenderness, decreased BP, fainting or blood in stool. G6PD deficiency, hepatic or renal dysfunction, Gilbert's syndrome, hepatocellular insufficiency (Child-Pugh A/B). Monitor blood count, renal & liver function after prolonged use. Discontinue use at 1st signs of hypersensitivity reaction. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use at high doses. Not to be taken for >3 days. Patients prone to narrow-angle glaucoma, susceptible to intestinal or urinary outlet obstructions & inclined to tachyarrhythmia. Patients on controlled Na diet. Not recommended during pregnancy. Lactation. Childn <10 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Pancytopenia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia; skin reactions, abnormal sweating, pruritus, urticaria, nausea, erythema, decreased BP including shock, anaphylactic shock, anaphylactic reactions, drug eruption, dyspnoea, hypersensitivity, angioedema, rash, exanthema; tachycardia; bronchospasm; dry mouth; increased transaminases; urinary retention. Paracetamol: SJS, TEN, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis.
Interactions: Hypnotics & antiepileptics (eg, glutethimide, phenobarb, phenytoin, carbamazepine); rifampicin; potentially hepatotoxic substances & alcohol. Intensified anticholinergic effects of tri- & tetracyclic antidepressants, antihistamines, antipsychotics, quinidine, amantadine, disopyramide & other anticholinergics (eg, tiotropium, ipratropium, atropine-like compd). Diminution of the effects of both drugs on GIT w/ dopamine antagonists eg, metoclopramide. Enhanced tachycardic effects of beta-adrenergic agents. Paracetamol: Long- term use w/ oral anticoagulants. Enhanced tendency of neutropenia w/ zidovudine. Concomitant use w/ probenecid. Reduced absorption w/ cholestyramine.
Presentation & Packing: FC tab 4's (P119), 100's (P3,125).

title: DIATABS (Antidiarrheals)
content:
DIATABS

Indications: Acute non-specific diarrhea; chronic diarrhea associated w/ inflammatory bowel disease. Reduction of number & vol of discharge in patients w/ ileostomies & colostomies.

title: DIATABS ADVANCE (Antidiarrheals)
content:
DIATABS ADVANCE
Manufacturer: Amherst Lab [UNILAB, Inc] — Non-Rx
Composition: Loperamide 2 mg, simeticone 125 mg
Indications: Relief of symptoms of diarrhea plus bloating, pressure & cramps, commonly referred to gas.

May cause loss/depressed level of consciousness, tiredness, dizziness, or drowsiness. Liver impairment. Use w/ special caution in young childn & those w/ compromised blood brain barrier (eg, meningitis). Pregnancy & lactation.
Adverse Reactions: Loperamide: Nausea, constipation, headache, abdominal cramps & pain, dizziness, dry mouth, dysgeusia (altered taste), vomiting, flatulence, dyspepsia, drowsiness, fatigue, urinary retention, difficulty urinating, distension, or discomfort.
Interactions: Loperamide: Increased plasma levels w/ ritonavir, quinidine, clarithromycin or erythromycin, quinine, itraconazole or ketoconazole, gemfibrozil. May increase constipating effect w/ medicines that reduce the action of stomach & intestines (eg, antidepressants & cold & allergy medications). May increase plasma levels w/ oral desmopressin. Composition: Loperamide HCl
Indications: Control & symptomatic relief of acute nonspecific diarrhea & chronic diarrhea associated w/ inflammatory bowel disease. Reduction of number & vol of discharge in patients w/ ileostomies & colostomies.
Dosage: Adult & childn over 12 yr Symptomatic relief of acute diarrhea Initially 2 cap followed by 1 cap after each loose bowel movement. Max: 16 mg daily (8 cap). Discontinue use if there is no improvement after 2 days. Symptomatic relief of chronic diarrhea Initially 2 cap followed by 1 cap after each loose bowel movement, then reduce dose to meet individual requirements. When optimal daily dose has been established, administer as a single dose or in divided doses. Ave daily maintenance dose: 2-4 cap daily. If no clinical improvement is observed after treatment w/ 8 cap daily (16 mg daily) for at least 10 days, symptoms are unlikely to be controlled.
Administration: Take with or without food.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Constipation, swollen abdomen or abdominal pain, acute dysentery characterized by blood in stools & high fever; pseudomembranous colitis, active ulcerative colitis, meningitis or history of liver disease. Pregnancy & lactation. Childn <12 yr.
Special Precautions: Appropriate fluid & electrolyte intake. Patients w/ AIDS should stop therapy at the earliest signs of abdominal distention. Toxic megacolon in AIDS patients w/ infectious colitis. Loss/depressed level of consciousness, tiredness, dizziness, or drowsiness may occur. Avoid alcohol or milk, fruits, green vegetables, & spicy or fatty foods. Childn.
Adverse Reactions: Dry mouth, abdominal pain, distention or discomfort, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, flatulence, constipation, epigastric pain, drowsiness & dizziness. Hypersensitivity reactions eg, pruritus, rashes, urticaria. Rarely, anaphylactic shock, angioedema & bullous eruptions including SJS, erythema multiforme, & TEN; paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, urinary retention, hypertonia, loss/depressed level of consciousness, coordination abnormality, & miosis.
Interactions: Increased plasma levels w/ ritonavir, quinidine, oral desmopressin, itraconazole or ketoconazole, gemfibrozil. Increased constipation w/ drugs that slow down the action of stomach & intestines (eg, drugs for depression & cold & allergy medications). Drugs causing drowsiness.
Presentation & Packing: Cap 2 mg x 100's (P780) (P7.80/cap).

title: DULCOLAX SUPPOSITORY (Laxatives, Purgatives)
content:
DULCOLAX SUPPOSITORY
Manufacturer: Opella Healthcare — Non-Rx
Composition: Bisacodyl
Indications: Constipation. Prep of diagnostic procedures, in pre- & post-op treatment & in conditions requiring defecation to be facilitated.
Dosage: Constipation Adult & childn >10 yr 1 adult supp daily. Childn 4-10 yr 1 ped supp daily, <4 yr 1 ped supp daily. Prep for diagnostic procedures, pre- & post-op treatment & conditions requiring defecation Adult 2-4 tab the night before, then 1 adult supp in the morning of exam. Childn ≥4 yr 1 tab the night before, then 1 ped supp on the following morning.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Ileus, intestinal obstruction, acute abdominal conditions including appendicitis, acute inflammatory bowel diseases & severe abdominal pain associated w/ nausea & vomiting; severe dehydration. Galactose/fructose intolerance, galactosaemia.
Special Precautions: Not to be taken on a continuous daily basis or for extended periods w/o investigating the cause of constipation. Prolonged excessive use may lead to fluid & electrolyte imbalance & hypokalaemia. Discontinue use & restart only under medical supervision in patients suffering from fluid loss where dehydration may be harmful. Does not help w/ wt loss. Haematochezia. Dizziness &/or syncope. Painful sensation & local irritation w/ supp use in patients w/ anal fissure & ulcerative proctitis. If patients experience abdominal spasm, avoid potentially hazardous tasks eg, driving or operating machinery. Renal insufficiency. Pregnancy. Childn. Elderly.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain & diarrhoea. Anaphylactic reactions, angioedema, hypersensitivity; dehydration; dizziness, syncope; abdominal cramps, nausea, haematochezia, vomiting, abdominal & anorectal discomfort, colitis eg, ischaemic colitis.
Interactions: Increased risk of electrolyte imbalance w/ (in excessive doses) diuretics & adrenocorticoids. Electrolyte imbalance may increase sensitivity to cardiac glycosides. May enhance GI side effects w/ other laxatives.
Presentation & Packing: Ped supp 5 mg x 50's (P1,486). Adult supp 10 mg x 50's (P1,532).

title: DUPHALAC (Laxatives, Purgatives)
content:
DUPHALAC
Manufacturer: Abbott — Non-Rx
Composition: Lactulose
Indications: Constipation: Regulation of physiological rhythm of the colon; where a soft stool is considered of medical benefit (hemorrhoids, post colonic/anal surgery). Hepatic encephalopathy: Treatment & prevention of hepatic coma or precoma in adults. Prebiotic: Helps create & maintain healthy intestinal balance & stimulates intestinal absorption of minerals like Ca & Mg in adults. Bowel cleansing in prep for colonoscopy in adults.
Dosage: Adult & adolescent Starting dose: 15-45 mL daily. Maintenance dose: 15-30 mL daily. Childn 7-14 yr Starting dose: 15 mL daily. Maintenance dose: 10-15 mL daily, 1-6 yr Starting & maintenance dose: 5-10 mL daily. Infant <1 yr Starting & maintenance dose: Up to 5 mL daily. Drink sufficient amounts of fluids (1.5-2 L, equal to 6-8 glasses) during the day. Hepatic encephalopathy Adult Starting dose: 20-30 g or 30-45 mL tid to qid. Prebiotic Adult 7.5-15 mL (corresponding to 5-10 g) daily. Bowel cleansing in prep for colonoscopy Adult Course of treatment consists of bisacodyl 10 mg in the evening before exam & Duphalac soln 1 L 6 hr before colonoscopy (eg, 1 hr after light breakfast on the day of exam). Dilute soln in order to obtain 12.5% lactulose soln by diluting 200 mL in 800 mL of water or lemon juice.
Administration: Swallow dose immediately, do not keep in mouth for an extended period of time. For single daily dose, take at the same time eg, during breakfast.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Galactosemia; GI obstruction, digestive perforation or risk of digestive perforation. Bowel cleansing: Not to be administered to unconscious patients or those w/ impaired consciousness & patients prone to aspiration or regurgitation, general weakness, w/ severe dehydration or impaired swallowing reflex.
Special Precautions: Painful abdominal symptoms of undetermined cause prior to treatment; insufficient therapeutic effect after several days. Diarrhea & disturbance of electrolyte balance in chronic use of unadjusted doses & misuse. Diabetics. Monitor electrolyte & fluid balance in patients at risk eg, elderly or debilitated. Not to be taken by patients w/ galactose or fructose intolerance, Lapp or total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption. Patients w/ lactose intolerance. Renal impairment. Newborn to 18 yr w/ hepatic encephalopathy. May disturb defecation reflex in childn. Bowel cleansing in childn.
Adverse Reactions: Diarrhea. Flatulence, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting.
Interactions: For bowel cleansing, orally administered medicines may be washed out of GI tract or may not or partially be absorbed several hr before, during or up to 1 hr after treatment. Enhanced GI side effects w/ other laxatives eg, bisacodyl.
Presentation & Packing: Syr (plain flavor) 3.3 g/5 mL x 45 mL (P208), 120 mL (P484).

content:
RITEMED BISACODYL

Indications: Short-term treatment of constipation or conditions where regular bowel movement is needed especially in bedridden patients. Bowel cleansing agent before surgery or other radiological procedures.
Dosage: Constipation Adult & childn >10 yr 5-10 mg as single dose usually in the evening. Childn 4-10 yr 5 mg as single dose usually in the evening. Should be taken on as needed basis & not to be taken everyday for >5 days. Prep for surgical or radiological procedures 10-20 mg on the night before the procedure.
Administration: Swallow whole, do not chew/crush. Do not take w/in 1 hr of antacids, milk or PPIs.

Special Precautions: Avoid prolonged use. Patients w/ inflammatory bowel disease. Sudden bowel changes for >2 wk. Pregnancy & lactation.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal discomfort eg, colic or cramps; diarrhea w/ depletion of fluid & electrolytes, malabsorption, wt loss w/ prolonged use; vomiting & muscle weakness. Rare cases of serious allergic reactions manifested as difficulty breathing; closing of throat; swelling of lips, tongue, or face; or hives & angioedema.
Interactions: May cause dyspepsia & gastric irritation w/ antacids (eg, Al hydroxide & Mg carbonate) & milk. May increase risk of electrolyte loss w/ corticosteroid (eg, prednisone, prednisolone) & diuretics (eg, furosemide, mannitol).

title: DOLFENAL (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs))

Diarrhea in the past w/ previous therapy. Cerebrovascular bleeding or other bleeding disorders. Known hyperkalemia. Dengue fever. Severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease. Pregnancy (3rd trimester) & lactation. Childn & adolescents <14 yr. 500 mg: GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAID therapy; previous or active ulceration or chronic inflammation of either the upper or lower GIT. Treatment of perioperative pain in the setting of CABG surgery. Asthma, urticaria, allergic-type reactions, severe, rarely fatal, anaphylactoid reactions to NSAIDs.

Not recommended for use w/ other NSAIDs except low-dose aspirin. Onset of new or worsening of preexisting HTN; closely monitor BP during initiation & throughout the course of therapy. Not to be used as substitute for corticosteroids. Serious GI adverse events including inflammation, bleeding, ulceration, & perforation of the stomach, small or large intestines. Prolonged use for headaches. Increased risk of aseptic meningitis in patients w/ SLE. Epilepsy. Liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or development of diarrhea should be monitored in patients on prolonged therapy. Not recommended in patients w/ advanced renal disease. May affect ability to drive or operate machinery. Pregnancy & lactation. Elderly patients suffering from impaired renal or hepatic cardiac function.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain, abnormal kidney function, anemia, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, edema, elevated liver enzymes (eg, ALT or AST), flatulence, GI ulcers (gastric/duodenal), gross bleeding/perforation, headache, heartburn, nausea, increased bleeding time, nausea, pruritus, rashes, tinnitus, & vomiting.

Increased risk of GI ulceration or bleeding w/ anticoagulants (eg, warfarin), antiplatelet agents (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel, cilostazol), corticosteroids & SSRIs (eg, fluoxetine, citalopram, sertraline). Increased adverse effects w/ aspirin, other NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, ketorolac, meloxicam) including COX-2 selective inhibitors (eg, celecoxib, etoricoxib). title: RITEMED MEFENAMIC ACID (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs))
content:
RITEMED MEFENAMIC ACID
Manufacturer: RiteMED [United Lab] — 250 mg: Non-Rx; 500 mg: Rx
Composition: Mefenamic acid
Indications: Relief of mild to moderate pain eg, headache, dental pain, pain after childbirth or surgery, primary dysmenorrhea, & menorrhagia (heavy menstrual period) due to dysfunctional causes. Relief of pain associated w/ musculoskeletal & joint disorders including OA & RA.
Dosage: Adult & childn >14 yr 1-2 tabs 250 mg tab or 1 tab 500 mg every 8 hr. Relief of dysmenorrhea & premenstrual syndrome 1-2 tabs 250 mg tab or 1 tab 500 mg every 8 hr, should not be given for >7 days.
Administration: Take immediately after meals.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity w/ mefenamic acid, aspirin or any other NSAID. Patient currently taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Patient had or is suffering from stomach ulcers, bleeding or other stomach problems eg, inflammatory bowel disease; diarrhea w/ mefenamic acid in the past. Severe heart, liver or kidney disease, bleeding in the brain or other bleeding disorders, high K in the blood, dengue fever. Pre- op pain in the setting of CABG surgery. Pregnancy (3rd trimester). Lactation. Childn & adolescent <14 yr. 250 mg: Bronchospasm, angioedema, nasal polyps or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. 500 mg: Asthma, urticaria.
Special Precautions: May increase risk of serious CV thrombotic events, MI, & stroke; patients w/ CV disease or risk factors for CV disease; ischemic heart disease (eg, MI &/or angina), cerebrovascular disease (eg, stroke, CVA, transient ischemic attacks &/or amaurosis fugax) &/or CHF. Serious GI adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, & perforation of the stomach, small or large intestines; increased stomach bleeding risk in patients w/ stomach ulcers or bleeding problems; taking blood thinning (anticoagulant) or steroid medicine; medicines containing prescription or nonprescription NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen or others); takes 3 or more alcoholic drinks everyday; prolonged use may increase risk of heart attack or stroke. Elderly patients suffering from dehydration & kidney disease. Not recommended for use w/ other NSAIDs, w/ the exception of low-dose aspirin for CV prophylaxis. Interferes w/ platelet function; used w/ caution in patients w/ intracranial hemorrhage & bleeding diathesis. Onset of new or worsening of preexisting HTN; closely monitor BP during initiation & throughout the course of therapy. Caution in patients w/ fluid retention or heart failure. Patients on prolonged corticosteroid therapy should be tapered slowly. Administration of NSAID may cause a dose-dependent reduction in prostaglandin formation & in renal blood flow which may precipitate overt renal decompensation. Patients at greater risk of are those w/ impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, taking diuretics & ACE inhibitors. Administer w/ caution to patients w/ preexisting asthma. Discontinue use at the 1st appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or any sign of hypersensitivity. Check for Hb or hematocrit in patients w/ long-term treatment w/ NSAIDs. Patients w/ symptoms &/or signs suggesting liver dysfunction, or in whom an abnormal liver test occurs should be evaluated. Discontinue if clinical signs & symptoms consistent w/ liver disease develop or if systemic manifestations occur (eg, eosinophilia, rash). Prolonged use of any types of analgesic may worsen headache. Increased risk of aseptic meningitis. Caution should be exercised in patients suffering from epilepsy. Liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or development of diarrhea should be monitored in patients on prolonged therapy. May affect the ability to drive & use machine. Not recommended in patients w/ advanced renal disease. Elderly. Childn & adolescent <14 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain, abnormal kidney function, anemia, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, edema, dizziness, elevated liver enzymes (eg, ALT or AST), flatulence, GI ulcers (gastric/duodenal), gross bleeding/perforation, headache, heartburn, increased bleeding time, itching, nausea, rashes, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), & vomiting.
Interactions: Increase risk of renal impairment w/ ACE inhibitors (eg, captopril, fosinopril, imidapril, enalapril) & AIIA (eg, losartan, telmisartan). May reduce excretion of aminoglycosides (eg, gentamicin) & MTX. Increased Cmax & AUC w/ antacid. Increased risk of ulceration or bleeding w/ anticoagulants (eg, warfarin), antiplatelet agents (eg, aspirin), corticosteroids & SSRIs (eg, fluoxetine, citalopram, sertraline). Increased adverse effects w/ aspirin, other NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, ketorolac, meloxicam) including COX-2 selective inhibitors (eg, celecoxib, etoricoxib). Reduced GFR & increase plasma cardiac glycoside levels w/ cardiac glycosides (eg, digoxin). Increased risk of nephrotoxicity w/ ciclosporin & tacrolimus. Reduced the natriuretic effects of diuretics (eg, thiazides, furosemide). Altered safety & efficacy w/ drugs affecting hepatic microsomal enzymes. Reduce renal excretion w/ lithium. Concomitant use w/ mifepristone can reduce its effects. Increased risk of hypoglycemia. Reduced metabolism & prolonged t½ w/ oral hypoglycemic agents (sulfonylureas eg, gliclazide, glipizide, glimepiride). Reduced metabolism & elimination w/ probenecid. Concomitant use w/ protein-bound drugs (eg, hydantoins, sulfonamides & sulfonylureas). Increased risk of convulsions w/ quinolones antibiotics. Increased risk of hematological toxicity w/ zidovudine.
Presentation & Packing: Tab 250 mg x 100's (P3.75/tab) (P375/box). 500 mg x 100's (P4.75/tab) (P475/box).

title: LESOFAT (Anti-Obesity Agents)
content:
LESOFAT
Manufacturer: Lloyd [Dr Zens Research] — Non-Rx
Composition: Orlistat
Indications: Obesity.
Dosage: 120 mg tid.
Administration: Take immediately before, during or w/in 1 hr after each main meal. If a meal is missed or contains no fat, the dose may be omitted.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to orlistat. Chronic malabsorption syndrome. Cholestasis. Lactation.
Special Precautions: Discontinue if patient does not lose at least 5% of their body wt during the 1st 12 wk of therapy. Long-term therapy should not continue beyond 2 yr. Wt loss may affect the dosing of medicines for other conditions (eg, high cholesterol or diabetes). Over- consumption of fat & cal may reduce wt loss effect. May increase GI effects if taken w/ a very high fat meal; daily intake of fat should be distributed evenly over 3 main meals. Renal stones in patients suffering from CKD. Use of additional contraceptive method to prevent possible failure of OCs in case of severe diarrhea. Not recommended during severe pregnancy & lactation. Not intended for childn.
Adverse Reactions: Headache, abdominal pain/discomfort, flatulence w/ or w/o discharge, oily discharge or fatty stools, low blood sugar levels, liqd stools, upper resp infections, flu. Rectal pain/discomfort, soft stools, incontinence, bloating, tooth/gum disorder, anxiety, lower resp infections, UTI.
Interactions: May modify the activity of anticoagulants (eg, warfarin), ciclosporin, iodine salts &/or levothyroxine, amiodarone, medicines for HIV. Reduced absorption of supplements of fat-soluble nutrients, particularly β-carotene & vit E. Decreased absorption of antiepileptic medicines. Acarbose.
Presentation & Packing: Cap 120 mg x 20's.

Abdominal pain/discomfort, flatulence, liqd stools, soft stools, rectal pain/discomfort, tooth disorder, gingival disorder. Rarely, elevated transaminase or alkaline phosphatase level or hepatitis.
Interactions: Inhibits absorption of oral fat soluble nutrient; decreased absorption of vit D, E & β-carotene. Reduction in cyclosporin plasma levels. Reduced therapeutic effect of amiodarone. Risk of convulsions w/ antiepileptic drugs. Warfarin or other oral anticoagulants. Increased GI events w/ high-fat diet.

title: BENADRYL ONE (Antihistamines & Antiallergics)

BENADRYL ONE
Manufacturer: Interphil [JNTL Consumer Health] — Non-Rx
Composition: Cetirizine HCl
Indications: Symptomatic relief of allergic conditions including rhinitis & chronic urticaria.
Dosage: Adult & childn ≥6 yr 10 mg daily. Seasonal rhinitis Give at beginning of hay fever season when pollens are still few. Hepatic & renal impairment Reduce dose to ½ of usual daily dose.
Administration: Take with or without food.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to cetirizine or hydroxyzine. Not recommended to hypokalemic patients w/ chronic renal failure undergoing hemodialysis. Not to be given to childn <6 yr w/ hepatic & renal impairment.
Special Precautions: Caution in patients who require mental alertness or physical coordination (eg, drivers or machine operators) since this may cause drowsiness. Pregnancy. Not recommended in lactating mothers. Not to be given to childn & infants. Elderly w/ most likely renal & hepatic impairment.

content:
BETADINE GARGLE/BETADINE PAINT/BETADINE THROAT SPRAY
Manufacturer: Interphil, Mundipharma Pharma [iNova] — Non-Rx
Composition: Povidone-iodine
Indications: Betadine Gargle: Fast & soothing relief of sore throat & mouth sores, breath freshener where excessive bacteria in mouth is present, mouth wash for oral hygiene & post-op or bedridden patients, oral antiseptic before & after dental operations, degerming soak for dentures & toothbrushes. Betadine Paint: Mouth sores (aphthous ulcers), herpes simplex, herpes zoster (shingles), herpes labialis (cold sores), grazes, abrasions, cuts & wounds, or any break in the skin which requires protection from infection. Betadine Throat Spray: Acute mucosal infections of the mouth & pharynx including stomatitis, gingivitis, aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, monilial infections, common colds & flu. Oral hygiene prior to, during, or after dental & oral surgery. Relief of sore throat.
Dosage: Betadine Gargle Sore throat & mouth infections Gargle undiluted 15 mL followed by mouth rinsing for min of 30 sec. Repeat 2-4 times daily or as required. Betadine Paint Apply undiluted to affected area bid. Betadine Throat Spray Spray to the mucous membrane of the throat several times a day (3-4 hrly).
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Hyperthyroidism or any thyroid diseases. Patients on lithium therapy. Before & after specific medical treatment involving use of radioactive iodine. Betadine Throat Spray: Do not use 4 wk prior to radio-iodine scintigraphy or radioiodine treatment of thyroid carcinoma. Patients w/ goiter & thyroid nodules. Childn <6 yr.
Special Precautions: Do not apply other medications to the same area treated. Avoid pooling beneath the patient in pre-op prep. Do not heat prior to use. Avoid contact w/ eyes & soln containing detergent in treating open wounds. Prolonged use. Patients w/ goiter, thyroid nodules & other non-acute thyroid diseases. Monitor thyroid function. Not to be used prior to or after radioiodine scintigraphy or radioiodine treatment of thyroid carcinoma. Renal impairment. False +ve lab results w/ toluidine or gum guaiac for Hb or glucose determination in stool or urine. May interfere w/ thyroid function tests. Pregnancy & lactation. Newborns & small infants. Betadine Throat Spray: Avoid aspiration into the resp tract especially in intubated patients.
Adverse Reactions: Rarely, hypersensitive/allergic skin reaction (itchiness, redness, small blisters).
Interactions: May alter the effect w/ other externally applied wound healing drugs/prep. Products containing enzymatic component, alkali, Hg, silver, hydrogen peroxide, tannic acid & taurolidine. Transient dark discolorations in areas involved in concomitant use or immediately after application of octenidine-containing antiseptics.
Presentation & Packing: Betadine Gargle 1% x 60 mL (P99.10), 120 mL (P167.59), 240 mL (P299.88), 500 mL (P520.73). Betadine Paint 10% x 10 mL (P156.05). Betadine Throat Spray 0.45% x 50 mL (P510.87).

Composition: Difflam: Benzydamine HCl 3 mg, cetylpyridinium Cl 1.33 mg. Difflam Mint/Difflam Lemon/Difflam Solution/Difflam Forte: Benzydamine HCl. Per 15 mL Difflam-C soln: Benzydamine HCl 22.5 mg, chlorhexidine gluconate 18 mg

Rinse for oral lesion 15 mL held in the mouth & swirled around for at least 30 sec repeated every 1½-3 hr throughout the day. Childn 6-12 yr 5-15 mL. Throat spray Adult & childn >12 yr 2-4 sprays. Childn 6-12 yr 2 sprays. Spray directly onto the sore/inflamed area & swallow gently. Repeat every 1½-3 hr as necessary.

Special Precautions: Do not swallow soln. Severe renal or hepatic impairment. Sensitization reaction w/ soln. Appropriate antibacterial therapy should be considered in bacterial infection complications. Excessive loz consumption may have laxative effect. Pregnancy. Not recommended in childn <6 yr. Difflam-C: Do not use in persons allergic to bee products (eg, propolis, honey, bee pollen). Persons w/ hypersensitivity conditions eg, allergies & asthma. Little burning sensation caused by alcoholic medium.
Adverse Reactions: Oral numbness; dryness or thirst, tingling, warm feeling in mouth, altered sense of taste. Systemic adverse reactions are very uncommon & are not serious in nature. Difflam-C: change in the mouth, on the tongue & teeth due to chlorhexidine. Renal or liver disorders. Not to be administered in childn <6 yr. Anaphylaxis (rare, life-threatening allergic reaction) & hypersensitivity; dry mouth, dysgeusia, tooth discoloration; erythema.

title: SOLMUX THROAT (Preparations for Oral Ulceration & Inflammation)
content:
SOLMUX THROAT
Manufacturer: UNILAB, Inc [Unilab Consumer Health] — Non-Rx
Composition: Per mL Benzydamine HCl 1.5 mg, chlorhexidine digluconate 1.2 mg
Indications: Relief of painful inflammatory conditions of throat including traumatic conditions eg, pharyngitis following tonsillectomy or use of nasogastric tube; inflammatory conditions eg, tonsillitis, sore throat, pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers & oral ulceration due to RT; after dental operations. Local antiseptic.
Dosage: Administer directly onto the sore or inflamed area. Repeat every 1½-3 hr as necessary. Adult & childn ≥12 yr 2-4 sprays. Childn 6- 12 yr 2 sprays.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Pregnancy or lactation.
Special Precautions: For symptomatic & short-term use only. Uninterrupted treatment should not exceed 7 days. Discontinue use if patient develops shortness of breath, skin rash, face &/or tongue swelling; hypersensitivity & allergic reactions; skin reactions due to irritation; mouth rash; throat irritation & cough; growing of salivary gland. Advise patient not to swallow & should be expectorated after each use. Not to be used w/o consulting a doctor if sore throat is severe or has lasted for >2 days or is accompanied by high fever, headache, nausea or vomiting. Antibiotic may be required if sore throat occurred w/ bacterial inflammation or accompanied by inflammation. Avoid contact w/ eyes & ears. Contains FD&C yellow #5 (tartrazine) which may cause allergic reactions (including bronchial asthma) in certain susceptible individuals. Contains alcohol in small amounts (<100 mg/dose). May lead to reversible color change in the mouth, on the tongue & teeth due to chlorhexidine. Renal or liver disorders. Not to be administered in childn <6 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Anaphylaxis (rare, life-threatening allergic reaction) & hypersensitivity; dry mouth, dysgeusia, tooth discoloration; erythema. Benzydamine: Angioedema; drowsiness; dizziness; headache; bronchospasm; cough, laryngospasm; nausea, oral mucosal stinging or sensation, retching, vomiting; photosensitivity, rash, pruritus, urticaria; thirst. Chlorhexidine: Ageusia, glossodynia, hypoesthesia, paresthesia, coated tongue, oral mucosal desquamation/swelling, tongue discoloration, gingivitis, glossitis, mucocele, sialadenosis, mouth irritation, parotid gland swelling; generalized allergic reactions.

title: STREPSILS MAXPRO DIRECT (Preparations for Oral Ulceration & Inflammation)
content:
STREPSILS MAXPRO DIRECT
Manufacturer: Reckitt Benckiser (Thailand) [Reckitt Benckiser] — Non-Rx
Composition: Flurbiprofen
Indications: Short-term relief of symptoms of sore throats eg, throat soreness, pain, difficulty swallowing & swelling.
Dosage: Adult & childn ≥12 yr 1 dose (3 sprays) to the back of the throat every 3-6 hr. Max: Not to exceed 5 doses (15 sprays) in 24 hr. Not to be used for >3 days.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to flurbiprofen, ibuprofen, ASA or other NSAIDs. Active or history of recurrent peptic ulcer/haemorrhage (≥2 distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding). History of GI bleeding or perforation, severe colitis, haemorrhagic or haematopoietic disorders related to previous NSAID therapy. Severe heart, hepatic or renal failure. Pregnancy (last trimester). Childn <12 yr.
Special Precautions: Discontinue use at 1st appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions or any other sign of hypersensitivity; if mouth irritation & GI bleeding or ulceration occurs. Not to be inhaled while spraying. For oromucosal & short-term use only. May have increased risk of aseptic meningitis in patients w/ SLE & mixed connective tissue disease. Nephrotoxicity. Analgesic-induced headache may occur in prolonged use or use beyond product posology. GI bleeding, ulceration & perforation. Isolated cases of exacerbation of infective inflammations eg, development of necrotizing fasciitis. Patients w/ history of bronchial asthma or allergic disease; renal & cardiac impairment, liver dysfunction; those taking diuretics & the elderly; history of HTN &/or heart failure; history of GI disease eg, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease. Avoid concomitant use w/ other NSAIDs including COX-2 selective inhibitors. Concomitant use w/ medications which could increase risk of ulceration or bleeding eg, oral corticosteroids, anticoagulants (eg, warfarin), SSRIs, or antiplatelet agents (eg, ASA). Limited evidence on impairment of female fertility. Avoid use during 1st & 2nd trimesters of pregnancy. Increased frequency of adverse reactions especially GI bleeding & perforation in the elderly.
Adverse Reactions: Dizziness, headache; throat irritation; mouth ulcers, pain, or numbness in the mouth; oropharyngeal pain; discomfort in the mouth; nausea & diarrhoea; itching sensation in skin.
Interactions: Risk of adverse reactions may be increased w/ low-dose ASA; other NSAIDs including ibuprofen & COX-2 selective inhibitors; alcohol. May enhance effects of anticoagulants eg, warfarin. Increased risk of GI bleeding w/ antiplatelet agents & SSRIs; corticosteroids. May reduce effect of diuretics & other antihypertensives eg, ACE inhibitors & AIIA. May exacerbate cardiac failure, reduce GFR & increase plasma glycoside levels w/ cardiac glycosides. Increased risk of nephrotoxicity w/ ciclosporin. Potential increases in plasma levels of lithium; MTX. Reduced effect of mifepristone. Increased risk of convulsions associated w/ quinolones. Possible increased risk of nephrotoxicity w/ tacrolimus. Increased risk of haematological toxicity w/ zidovudine.
Presentation & Packing: Oromucosal spray (mint & cherry flavor) 8.75 mg/0.5 mL x 15 mL x 1's.
